questions: Test the remote rollback on a batch of real field units (or at least ones in the test lab with the same hardware): does a downgrade to the previous firmware complete, and what share fails or stays offline?

Pull the 200 field-trial units' list: what were their locations, outdoor temperatures during the two weeks (minimum and longest stretch below 0 C), and compressor hardware revisions, compared with the same breakdown of the 40,000 installed base?

Ask the compressor supplier for the written basis of their sign-off: was it a model calculation or a physical endurance test, how many start/stop cycles and defrost cycles were run, and at what temperatures?

Does the lab suite include sustained sub-zero operation, restart after defrost and short-cycling checks for the new compressor logic? Read the test list for those cases and run them in a climate chamber if they are missing.

Which telemetry signals show a lockout, a protection trip or a failed restart within an hour of it happening, and how long is the delay between a unit's event and it reaching the dashboard? Check with a deliberately triggered test fault.
Did any of the last six updates change compressor control or defrost logic? Open their release notes and compare the changed modules with this release.

How many units sit on weak connectivity or old bootloaders, and has the update process been tested with interrupted flashes (power or connection loss mid-update) to confirm units recover and do not stay in a boot loop?
Ask a sample of installers which custom settings they use (weather-compensation curves, buffer tank setups) and run the new firmware against the three or four most common ones on a test rig.

Check the support team's forecast: how many calls per hour does the campaign launch alone typically generate, and what is the number of extra calls per hour if even 1% of the units have a problem? Can staffing be extended on Monday and Tuesday?
Can the rollout be staged in waves (for example 1%, then 10%, then the rest) with a defined stop rule, and does the update server support pausing mid-wave?

lean.option: Roll out to all units on Monday
lean.reasons: The firmware passed the lab suite and a two-week field trial, the last six updates went smoothly, customers want the energy-saving mode, and the Monday marketing launch is already set.

premortem: The 200-unit field trial ran in mild weather; at sustained sub-zero temperatures, the new compressor control logic short-cycles or fails to restart after defrost, and units lock out in the first cold snap.

The trial units were mostly one or two hardware revisions; older units with a different compressor batch or sensor calibration respond differently to the new control logic, and a fraction trip protection and stop heating.

The update process itself fails on units with weak connectivity; a partial flash leaves some units stuck in a boot loop, and the support team, staffed for a normal week, is flooded with calls on Monday.

The energy-saving mode interacts with installers' custom settings (for example, weather-compensation curves or buffer tank configurations) that were not represented in the trial, so homes cool down overnight.

There is no remote way to roll units back to the prior firmware, so when the compressor supplier finds a wear problem from the new control pattern after a few weeks, the fix requires a technician visit to many thousands of homes.

beliefs.belief: The firmware is safe because it passed the full lab test suite.
beliefs.rests_on: The test suite results and sign-off.
beliefs.how_wrong: The lab suite tests cases someone anticipated; the changed compressor logic may fail in conditions the suite does not include, such as long cold spells or unusual installation setups.

beliefs.belief: The 200-unit field trial represents the 40,000 installed units.
beliefs.how_wrong: The trial covered a small, possibly volunteer or friendly sample, ran two weeks, and may not include cold regions, older hardware revisions or varied installers.

beliefs.belief: The compressor logic change is safe for the compressor over its lifetime.
beliefs.rests_on: The compressor supplier's involvement and agreement.
beliefs.how_wrong: Supplier sign-off may be based on a model rather than long-run testing; wear effects appear over months, not within a two-week trial.

beliefs.belief: Past smooth updates predict a smooth rollout this time.
beliefs.rests_on: The record of six incident-free firmware updates.
beliefs.how_wrong: Those updates probably did not touch compressor control; a track record from lower-risk changes does not carry over to this one.

beliefs.belief: If problems appear, the team will see them quickly and can stop the rollout.
beliefs.rests_on: Telemetry dashboards and customer support reports.
beliefs.how_wrong: Telemetry may not capture lockouts or comfort complaints in real time, and an all-at-once push leaves no time to stop before every unit is updated.

beliefs.belief: Units can be rolled back remotely if something goes wrong.
beliefs.rests_on: A general assumption about the update system's capabilities.
beliefs.how_wrong: Rollback may never have been tested on field units, and some may not support downgrade or may be offline.

beliefs.belief: Support is adequately staffed for the launch week.
beliefs.rests_on: The standard staffing plan for a normal week.
beliefs.how_wrong: The marketing campaign and any firmware-related issues will push contact volume far above a normal week.
